# The Foreigner Over the Mountain: A Speculative Archaeolinguistic Inquiry

---

In mid-20th-century America, two famous Wallaces—Henry A. Wallace, FDR's idealistic VP, and Mike Wallace, CBS *60 Minutes* correspondent—had unrelated roots: Henry from Ulster-Scots Presbyterian Iowa; Mike from Russian-Jewish immigrants who anglicized *Wallechinsky*. Their shared surname seems a melting-pot quirk. Zooming out to deep Eurasian time reveals a haunting mirror: Cantonese **Wài-lái (外来, wai6 loi4)** means 'outsider/foreigner.' **Wallace** derives from Old Norman French *Waleis* ('Welshman/foreigner'), from Proto-Germanic ***walhaz**—a foreigner, Celt, or Roman, likely from Celtic *Volcae*. **Wallace** and **Wài-lái** encode the same semantic core: *the one from outside*. Mainstream linguistics rightly calls this a false cognate, but speculative archaeolinguistics suggests both encode the same Bronze Age social reality: settled farmers naming people from over the mountains.

---

## The 4th-Century Continental Shattering

- **East:** Western Jin collapse → **Yongjia Disaster (永嘉之乱, 311 AD)**; Xiongnu and northern nomads shattered the heartland; elites, peasants, and merchants fled south in **Yiguan Nandu (衣冠南渡)**. Refugees settled the Yangtze basin; later waves carried Sinitic speech into Fujian, Guangdong, and Taiwan, shielding it from northern shifts.

- **West:** **Völkerwanderung** tore Rome apart; Huns—often linked to the same Xiongnu confederation—pushed Germanic tribes west, driving Anglo-Saxons to Britain, where they isolated Celts and called them ***walhaz** ('foreigners').

---

## The Shadow of the Steppe Network

How did fleeing populations across Eurasia develop symmetrical concepts of 'outsider'? A speculative bridge: the deep-time steppe network before Xiongnu/Huns shattered it. Long before the Silk Road, pastoralists and traders—including **Tocharians** in the Tarim Basin (linked to Tarim Mummies)—moved horses, wheels, and metallurgy. Tocharian was Centum Indo-European, closer to Celtic/Germanic than neighbors. Mainstream linguistics rejects a unified 'Eurasian trade language,' but accepts deep-time contact: Old Chinese *蜜* (*mit*; cf. English *mead*) and *犬* (*kʷʰen*; cf. *canine/hound*) plausibly spread in this prehistoric synthesis. In the shared matrix of settled oasis/valley vs. mobile steppe, the outsider archetype was forged.

---

## The Disappearing Phantom

Southern evidence cuts both ways. **Hokkien** preserves archaic features—glottal-stop finals, ancient 疑母 initial—and pronounces the word **gōa-lâi**, with a voiced velar stop from Old Chinese velar nasal ***ŋ-**. The more archaic the pronunciation, the less it resembles *Wallace*. Even Cantonese **wai6 loi4** acquired *w-* only when older *ŋw-* lost its nasal within the last millennium. In rapid modern speech [g] may soften toward [w], but historically the resemblance is a young coincidence. Strip away sound, and the fossil remains: both ***walhaz** and **Wài-lái** were coined by settled agriculturalists—wheat farmers on the Yellow River, barley farmers on the Rhine—naming the same figure: *the one who comes from over the mountain*. The phonetic twin is a phantom; the semantic twin is 4,000 years old.

---

## The Model and the Last Witness

The disappearing phantom has a contemporary counterpart. The minority languages that preserve the older phonological layers—Hokkien with its retained *ŋ-, Hakka with its nasal initial, Cantonese with its transitional w-—are also among the least represented in the training corpora of large language models. LLMs are not neutral archives. They are statistical engines trained overwhelmingly on standard Mandarin, standard English, and other dominant written languages; their tokenizers, spell-checkers, and “grammar correction” functions are optimized for those standards. When a model meets a dialect form, it may normalize it, translate it into the standard, or flag it as an error. In that moment, the model does not simply fail to preserve the minority language. It reinforces the hierarchy in which the standard is the only legitimate voice.

This matters for our fossil. The semantic twin between *walhaz and wài-lái survives in meaning, but the phonetic evidence that lets us date the divergence—the *ŋ- that Hokkien kept, the ŋw- that Cantonese shed—lives in communities already under pressure from standardized schooling, mass media, and migration, communities that history books have already sidelined and that digital archives may now flatten. If those communities lose their speech, the historical record does not merely become poorer; it becomes flatter. We will still have the dictionary entry for “foreigner.” We will have lost the accent in which the word was first spoken. And if the next generation’s model is trained mostly on the flattened standard, it will reproduce that loss with perfect confidence and call it correctness.

None of this makes LLMs the cause of language death. The causes are older and more material: schooling, labor markets, borders, stigma. But LLMs are a new amplifier. They can scale the standard and silence the variant at a speed no school system ever could. The phantom in this essay is therefore double. It is the false cognate between Wallace and wài-lái—and it is the possibility that the last witnesses to the older layers will be archived, tokenized, and “corrected” out of the record. The semantic fossil may remain. The phonetic ghost may not.

---

## The Elevator in the Tower

Embedding spaces are where the Babel question becomes technical. A multilingual model places the vector for “foreigner,” the vector for 外来, and the vector for *walhaz near one another—not because they share a root, but because they share a distribution of contexts. In the geometry of the model, semantic twins are pulled together across scripts and language families. If Babel means the scattering of tongues, embeddings look like a partial reversal: a space where meaning can be compared without passing through any single language.

But look more closely at Wallace. In a modern corpus, the token “Wallace” is overwhelmingly a surname—a vice president, a television interviewer, a border wall, a line from a poem. Its vector is pulled toward the semantic neighborhood of proper nouns, people, places, institutions, and away from the neighborhood of “foreigner” or “outsider.” The etymological trace is not absent from the model; it is drowned out by four thousand years of subsequent usage. The model has no reason to weight the Proto-Germanic root over the twentieth-century celebrity. So the embedding space does not simply fail to recover the ancient semantic twin. It actively reproduces the modern narrative in which Wallace is just a name, and the older sense of “the one from over the mountain” survives only as a low-magnitude direction that the next fine-tuning run can overwrite. The historical linguist can bracket the modern surname and dig for *walhaz. The embedding model cannot easily bracket anything; it compresses the whole distribution, and the distribution is dominated by the present. This is the first way AI amplifies the erasure—not by deleting the ancient trace, but by making the modern usage so dominant that the trace becomes statistically invisible.

The obvious reply is that pure-text LLMs are already being supplemented by speech models. Frontier labs are collecting oral corpora at scale—dialect recordings, conversational speech, endangered-language fieldwork—precisely because text alone misses what is spoken. Multimodal models can in principle hear the *ŋ- that Hokkien preserved, the nasal initial that standard Mandarin lost, the tonal contours that a written standard flattens. This looks like the correction the previous section called for: capture the phonological ghost before it disappears.

In practice, the same standardization pressure reappears one layer down, and it does not operate identically across writing systems. For a language written alphabetically, the problem of dialect is largely a problem of orthography: there is no agreed standard spelling, so the model either invents one or forces the dialect into the standard language’s spelling conventions. The sounds may survive in the spelling, even if the words are reshaped. For a language written in Chinese characters, the problem is deeper. A dialect word often has no character that matches both its sound and its meaning; the spoken grammar may not fit the syntax of modern standard written Chinese at all. Transcribing Hokkien into standard Mandarin characters is therefore not a matter of picking a standard spelling. It is a matter of re-encoding the utterance at the lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic levels—replacing the dialect’s own words and constructions with standard Chinese equivalents that mean roughly the same thing. The *ŋ- is captured in the audio, but the text layer—the layer most downstream systems actually use—has already discarded it, along with the expressions and collocations that made the dialect a distinct way of speaking rather than a deviant way of pronouncing the standard.

This asymmetry matters for how we read the multimodal correction. Speech models widen the intake; they do not remove the hierarchy that decides which layer counts as the real record. A pipeline that hears everything and transcribes it into the standard has preserved the acoustics and lost the language. And because the mapping from multimodal corpus to embedding is harder for character-written dialects than for alphabetically written ones—more information has to be thrown away at the text layer—the erasure is deeper precisely where the historical trace is older. The tools built to preserve the record can complete the erasure by transcribing it into the standard and filing the original as noise.

So the Babel metaphor needs to be stated more carefully. LLMs do not undo the scattering of tongues, and they should not be asked to. What they offer is an elevator inside the tower: a way to move between floors without learning each floor’s language, while the floors themselves remain distinct. That is a real good, and it is not nothing. But the elevator’s buttons are labeled in the dominant language, and the voice channel is normalized to the standard accent. The risk is not that AI will flatten all languages into one. The risk is that cross-lingual meaning will become so frictionless that the loss of phonological, lexical, and syntactic specificity stops registering as a loss at all—and that the very tools built to preserve the record will finish the job by translating it into the standard and calling the result correct.

---

## The Ghost in the Studio

When Myron Wallechinsky's father arrived at Ellis Island and shortened the name to **Wallace**, he chose an Anglo-Saxon moniker to blend into New York, thinking he adopted a Scottish borders name. He could not know he was invoking an ancient pan-Eurasian psychological structure. Next time you watch Mike Wallace grill a politician or read about Henry Wallace, look past the studio lights: the name encodes a 4,000-year-old trauma shared by the Rhine and Yellow River—the settled farmer's shadow watching the dark steppe, awaiting **the foreigner from over the mountain**, a fear unchanged even as language shifts beneath our feet.
